The Python companion to the deck. Steps 1–3 are the code of slides 31–33; Steps 4–9 follow the deck from the two small shops (Parts 2 and 3) to the real series (Part 4). The file sits in `sessions/01-foundations/`, so it reads the data two folders up (`../../data/forecasting/`):

- `hand_examples.csv`: the two invented shops. Column `example` is `contracts` (a phone shop, new mobile contracts per week, weeks 1–8) or `webshop` (a chocolate web shop, sales per quarter in k EUR, quarters 1–12); `period` is the week or quarter, `value` the number.
- `aus_clothing_retail.csv`: clothing sales in Australia, one row per month from April 1982 to April 2019 (`month`, `value` = turnover in AUD m, not seasonally adjusted). Source: ABS, Retail Trade, Australia (8501.0), Table 11; CC BY 4.0. We use 2009–2018: 2009–2016 to fit, 2017–2018 as the holdout.

The in-class exercise, `forecasting_exercise.qmd`, reuses these steps on the cafés series (`aus_cafes_retail.csv`).

## Step 1: load, split and plot

The code of slide 31. The filter keeps 2009–2018; the rows are in time order, so the last 24 months are the holdout (never split a time series at random).

```{python}
import polars as pl
from plotnine import aes, geom_line, ggplot

df = (pl.read_csv("../../data/forecasting/"
                  "aus_clothing_retail.csv",
                  try_parse_dates=True)
      .filter(pl.col("month").dt.year()
              .is_between(2009, 2018)))
y = df["value"].to_numpy()
train, test = y[:-24], y[-24:]   # 2017-18

(ggplot(df, aes("month", "value"))
 + geom_line())
```

The split, the lowest and highest month, and the sales per year: the year totals show the trend without the season, flat until 2012 (a cycle) and then about +4 % a year (slides 22 and 23).

```{python}
# the split, the extremes and the year totals
print(len(y), "months:", len(train), "to fit,", len(test), "to test")
print(df.filter(pl.col("value").is_in([y.min(), y.max()])))
years = (df.group_by(year=pl.col("month").dt.year())
         .agg(total=pl.col("value").sum())
         .sort("year"))
totals = years["total"].to_numpy()
print("growth 2009-2018, %:", round(100 * (totals[-1] / totals[0] - 1), 1))
print("growth a year 2012-2018, %:", round(100 * ((totals[-1] / totals[3]) ** (1 / 6) - 1), 1))
years
```

## Step 2: Holt-Winters and SARIMA

The code of slide 32. `seasonal="mul"` is the multiplicative Holt-Winters model of slide 25; `np.resize(train[-12:], 24)` repeats the last training year twice (the seasonal naive); SARIMA works on log sales, and `np.exp()` brings its forecast back to AUD m.

```{python}
import numpy as np
import statsmodels.tsa.api as tsa

hw = tsa.ExponentialSmoothing(
    train, trend="add", seasonal="mul",
    seasonal_periods=12,
    initialization_method="estimated").fit()
sar = tsa.SARIMAX(
    np.log(train), order=(0, 1, 1),
    seasonal_order=(0, 1, 1, 12),
).fit(disp=0)

fc = {"snaive": np.resize(train[-12:], 24),
      "hw": hw.forecast(24),
      "sarima": np.exp(sar.forecast(24))}
```

The fitted weights of Holt-Winters (α level, β trend, γ season; γ = 0 means it keeps the seasonal pattern it started with) and SARIMA's two memory terms (θ last month, Θ last year), as in the table of slide 32:

```{python}
# fitted weights and terms
print("alpha:", round(hw.params["smoothing_level"], 3))
print("beta:", round(hw.params["smoothing_trend"], 3))
print("gamma:", round(hw.params["smoothing_seasonal"], 3))
print("theta, Theta:", sar.params[:2].round(3))
```

## Step 3: regression on log sales and the accuracy table

The code of slide 33. `t` counts the months 1 … 120 and `C(m)` turns the month number into 11 dummies (January is the baseline). `pl.DataFrame(fc)` puts the four forecasts side by side, one column per method; `pl.all()` means "every column", so each line computes one measure of slide 19 for all methods at once. `a` holds the absolute errors |actual − forecast|; their mean, `a.mean()`, is the MAE; RMSE squares them, MAPE divides them by the actual.

```{python}
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

d = df.with_columns(
    t=pl.int_range(1, pl.len() + 1),
    m=pl.col("month").dt.month()).to_pandas()
reg = smf.ols("np.log(value) ~ t + C(m)",
              data=d[:-24]).fit()
fc["reg_log"] = np.exp(reg.predict(d[-24:]))

f = pl.DataFrame(fc)  # a column per method
a = f.select((pl.all() - test).abs())
rmse = a.select((pl.all() ** 2).mean().sqrt())
mape = a.select(pl.all() / test).mean() * 100
acc = pl.concat([a.mean(), rmse, mape])
acc.select(pl.all().round(1))  # MAE RMSE MAPE
```

How to read it: the three rows are MAE, RMSE and MAPE (%). Only the log regression (MAE 54.5 AUD m) beats the seasonal naive (67.2); SARIMA (94.9) and Holt-Winters (96.6) do not. Step 7 adds eleven more methods.

## Step 4: simple forecasts by hand

**The phone shop.** The by-hand forecasts of Part 2 (slides 11–14): new contracts in weeks 1–8; we forecast week 9 with naive (the last value), drift (the last value + the average change), the mean and the moving average of the last 3 weeks.

```{python}
# the two shops (20 rows) and four forecasts of week 9
hand = pl.read_csv("../../data/forecasting/hand_examples.csv")
phone = hand.filter(pl.col("example") == "contracts")["value"].to_numpy()
slope = (phone[-1] - phone[0]) / (len(phone) - 1)            # the average change per week
print("changes:", np.diff(phone), " mean change:", slope, " naive:", phone[-1])
print("drift:", phone[-1] + slope, " week 10:", phone[-1] + 2 * slope)
print("mean:", phone.sum(), "/ 8 =", phone.mean(), " moving average (3):", phone[-3:].mean())
hand
```

Simple exponential smoothing (slide 13): level = α × value + (1 − α) × old level, starting with the first value; the forecast is the last level. statsmodels does it with a fixed α (`optimized=False`) and the first value as the start (`initialization_method="known"`); `.level` is the level after each week, `.fittedvalues` the forecast made the week before.

```{python}
# simple exponential smoothing with alpha 0.5, 0.2 and 1
model = tsa.SimpleExpSmoothing(phone, initialization_method="known", initial_level=phone[0])
ses5 = model.fit(smoothing_level=0.5, optimized=False)
ses2 = model.fit(smoothing_level=0.2, optimized=False)
ses1 = model.fit(smoothing_level=1, optimized=False)
print("forecast week 9, alpha 0.5:", ses5.forecast(1))
print("alpha 0.2 levels:", ses2.level.round(2), " forecast:", ses2.forecast(1).round(2))
print("alpha 1 (= naive):", ses1.forecast(1))
pl.DataFrame({"week": range(1, 9), "contracts": phone, "level": ses5.level, "forecast": ses5.fittedvalues})
```

The trend regression (slide 14): b1 = sum (t − t̄)(y − ȳ) / sum (t − t̄)², then b0 = ȳ − b1 × t̄; `smf.ols` gives the same.

```{python}
# regression on time: contracts = b0 + b1 * t
t = np.arange(1, 9)
print("t mean:", t.mean(), " sum (t - tbar)^2:", ((t - t.mean()) ** 2).sum())
print("sum (t - tbar)(y - ybar):", ((t - t.mean()) * (phone - phone.mean())).sum())
weeks = hand.filter(pl.col("example") == "contracts").rename({"period": "t"}).to_pandas()
trend = smf.ols("value ~ t", data=weeks).fit()
print("R² = 1 -", round(trend.ssr, 2), "/", round(trend.centered_tss, 2), "=", round(trend.rsquared, 3))
print("weeks 9 and 10:", trend.predict(pl.DataFrame({"t": [9, 10]}).to_pandas()).round(2).to_list())
trend.params.round(2)
```

**The chocolate shop.** Sales per quarter for three years (slide 15). The seasonal effect of a quarter is its average gap to the year mean.

```{python}
# each quarter's gap to its year mean; the seasonal effect is the average gap
shop = (hand.filter(pl.col("example") == "webshop")
        .with_columns(year=(pl.col("period") - 1) // 4 + 1,
                      quarter=(pl.col("period") - 1) % 4 + 1)
        .with_columns(year_total=pl.col("value").sum().over("year"),
                      year_mean=pl.col("value").mean().over("year"))
        .with_columns(gap=pl.col("value") - pl.col("year_mean")))
print(shop.pivot(on="quarter", index=["year", "year_total", "year_mean"], values="value"))
print(shop.pivot(on="quarter", index="year", values="gap"))
shop.group_by("quarter").agg(seasonal_effect=pl.col("gap").mean()).sort("quarter")
```

Two forecasts for year 4 (slide 16): the seasonal naive repeats year 3; the seasonal regression adds a trend and quarter dummies (Q1 is the baseline), so Q4 of year 4 is 19 + 1 × 16 + 8 = 43.

```{python}
# year 4: seasonal naive and seasonal regression
quarters = shop.rename({"period": "t"}).to_pandas()
reg_q = smf.ols("value ~ t + C(quarter)", data=quarters).fit()
year4 = pl.DataFrame({"t": [13, 14, 15, 16], "quarter": [1, 2, 3, 4]}).to_pandas()
q = shop["value"].to_numpy()
print("seasonal naive:", q[8:], " with drift:", q[8:] + (q[8:] - q[:4]) / 2)
print("seasonal regression:", reg_q.predict(year4).round(2).to_list(), " R²:", round(reg_q.rsquared, 3))
reg_q.params.round(2)
```

## Step 5: how good is a forecast?

The holdout of Part 3 (slides 18–20): fit on weeks 1–5, forecast weeks 6–8 and compare with what happened. The error is actual − forecast.

```{python}
# forecasts of weeks 6-8 from weeks 1-5
tr = phone[:5]
fit5 = smf.ols("value ~ t", data=weeks[:5]).fit()
ses_tr = tsa.SimpleExpSmoothing(tr, initialization_method="known", initial_level=tr[0]).fit(
    smoothing_level=0.5, optimized=False)
hold = pl.DataFrame({
    "week": [6, 7, 8], "actual": phone[5:],
    "naive": tr[-1], "drift": tr[-1] + np.array([1, 2, 3]) * (tr[-1] - tr[0]) / 4,
    "mean": tr.mean(), "ma3": tr[-3:].mean(), "ses": ses_tr.forecast(1)[0],
    "trend regression": fit5.predict(weeks[5:]).to_numpy()})
print("trend regression, weeks 1-5: b0, b1 =", fit5.params.round(2).to_list())
hold
```

The errors of all six methods, with the naive rows as on slide 19; MAE, RMSE and MAPE are the column means (RMSE the root of the mean squared error), best first as on slide 20.

```{python}
# errors by hand, then MAE, RMSE and MAPE of all six methods
errors = (hold.unpivot(index=["week", "actual"], variable_name="method", value_name="forecast")
          .with_columns(error=pl.col("actual") - pl.col("forecast"))
          .with_columns(abs_error=pl.col("error").abs(), squared=pl.col("error") ** 2,
                        pct=100 * pl.col("error").abs() / pl.col("actual")))
print(errors.filter(pl.col("method") == "naive"))
(errors.group_by("method")
 .agg(mean_error=pl.col("error").mean(), MAE=pl.col("abs_error").mean(),
      squared=pl.col("squared").mean(), RMSE=pl.col("squared").mean().sqrt(), MAPE=pl.col("pct").mean())
 .sort("MAE")
 .with_columns(pl.col(pl.Float64).round(2)))
```

For the chocolate shop, fit on years 1–2 and forecast year 3 (28, 24, 26, 40):

```{python}
# the chocolate shop: MAE on year 3
reg_q8 = smf.ols("value ~ t + C(quarter)", data=quarters[:8]).fit()
print("naive:", np.abs(q[8:] - q[7]).mean())
print("mean:", np.abs(q[8:] - q[:8].mean()).mean())
print("seasonal naive:", np.abs(q[8:] - q[4:8]).mean())
print("seasonal regression:", np.abs(q[8:] - reg_q8.predict(quarters[8:]).to_numpy()).mean().round(2))
```

How to read it: only the trend regression (MAE 1.20) beats naive (2.67), because the averages lag behind the trend. With a season, naive (8.00) and the mean (6.00) miss Christmas: the benchmark for seasonal data is the seasonal naive (4.00).

## Step 6: decomposition and stationarity

STL splits the clothing series into trend, season and remainder (slide 23); `robust=True` keeps one-off months from bending the trend.

```{python}
# STL: trend, season and remainder
from plotnine import facet_wrap, labs
stl = tsa.STL(y, period=12, robust=True).fit()
print("strength of trend:", round(1 - np.var(stl.resid) / np.var(stl.trend + stl.resid), 2))
print("strength of season:", round(1 - np.var(stl.resid) / np.var(stl.seasonal + stl.resid), 2))
print("December swing 2009:", stl.seasonal[11].round(1), " 2018:", stl.seasonal[-1].round(1))
parts = (pl.DataFrame({"month": df["month"], "trend": stl.trend, "season": stl.seasonal,
                       "remainder": stl.resid})
         .unpivot(index="month", variable_name="part"))
(ggplot(parts, aes("month", "value")) + geom_line()
 + facet_wrap("part", ncol=1, scales="free_y") + labs(x="", y="AUD m"))
```

The December swing grows with the level, so the season is multiplicative: one seasonal index per month (1.59 = December sells 59 % more than an average month).

```{python}
# seasonal index per month (classical multiplicative decomposition)
index = tsa.seasonal_decompose(y, model="multiplicative", period=12).seasonal[:12]
december = df.filter(pl.col("month").dt.month() == 12)["value"].to_numpy()
print("December share of the year, %:", round(100 * (december / totals).mean(), 1))
print("December 2018 vs November 2018, %:", round(100 * (y[-1] / y[-2] - 1), 1))
pl.DataFrame({"month": range(1, 13), "index": index.round(3)})
```

The ADF test (slide 24) asks whether the series wanders without a fixed mean: a small p (< 0.05) says stationary. Differencing is the fix: the change on last month (`np.diff`) and on the same month last year; SARIMA takes both inside.

```{python}
# ADF p-values: levels, log and the differences
log_y = np.log(y)
both = np.diff(log_y[12:] - log_y[:-12])
print("levels:", round(tsa.adfuller(y)[1], 4))
print("log:", round(tsa.adfuller(log_y)[1], 4))
print("change on last month:", round(tsa.adfuller(np.diff(y))[1], 4))
print("change on last year:", round(tsa.adfuller(y[12:] - y[:-12])[1], 4))
print("both changes, log:", round(tsa.adfuller(both)[1], 4), " KPSS p:", tsa.kpss(both, nlags="auto")[1])
```

## Step 7: all fifteen methods on the holdout

Slide 26 compares fifteen methods on 2017–2018. Five more simple ones, each one line, added to the `fc` of Steps 2 and 3:

```{python}
# five more simple methods (the seasonal naive is in Step 2)
h = np.arange(1, 25)                     # 1 to 24 months ahead
fc["naive"] = np.repeat(train[-1], 24)
fc["drift"] = train[-1] + h * (train[-1] - train[0]) / (len(train) - 1)
fc["mean"] = np.repeat(train.mean(), 24)
fc["ma3"] = np.repeat(train[-3:].mean(), 24)
fc["ma12"] = np.repeat(train[-12:].mean(), 24)
print("naive = December 2016:", train[-1], " drift slope:", round((train[-1] - train[0]) / (len(train) - 1), 2))
print("months the log regression forecast too low:", (test > fc["reg_log"]).sum(), "of 24")
```

Four smoothing models (simple exponential smoothing, Holt with a trend, additive Holt-Winters, ETS) and two more regressions:

```{python}
# smoothing models and regressions in levels
ses = tsa.SimpleExpSmoothing(train, initialization_method="estimated").fit()
holt = tsa.ExponentialSmoothing(train, trend="add", initialization_method="estimated").fit()
fc["ses"] = ses.forecast(24)
fc["holt"] = holt.forecast(24)
fc["hw_add"] = tsa.ExponentialSmoothing(train, trend="add", seasonal="add", seasonal_periods=12,
                                        initialization_method="estimated").fit().forecast(24)
fc["ets_mam"] = tsa.ETSModel(train, error="mul", trend="add", seasonal="mul",
                             seasonal_periods=12).fit(disp=False).forecast(24)
fc["reg"] = smf.ols("value ~ t + C(m)", data=d[:-24]).fit().predict(d[-24:])
fc["reg_trend"] = smf.ols("value ~ t", data=d[:-24]).fit().predict(d[-24:])
print("SES alpha:", round(ses.params["smoothing_level"], 3))
print("Holt alpha, beta:", round(holt.params["smoothing_level"], 3), round(holt.params["smoothing_trend"], 3))
```

The table, best first (`hw` is the multiplicative Holt-Winters of Step 2, `reg_log` the log regression of Step 3, `ets_mam` ETS (M,A,M)); the mean error is actual − forecast, so a negative one means the forecast was too high.

```{python}
# MAE, RMSE, MAPE and mean error of all fifteen methods
from great_tables import GT
holdout = (pl.DataFrame(fc).with_columns(actual=test)
           .unpivot(index="actual", variable_name="method", value_name="forecast")
           .with_columns(error=pl.col("actual") - pl.col("forecast"))
           .group_by("method")
           .agg(MAE=pl.col("error").abs().mean(), RMSE=(pl.col("error") ** 2).mean().sqrt(),
                MAPE=(100 * pl.col("error").abs() / pl.col("actual")).mean(),
                mean_error=pl.col("error").mean())
           .sort("MAE"))
(GT(holdout).fmt_number(columns=["MAE", "RMSE", "MAPE", "mean_error"], decimals=1)
 .tab_header(title="Holdout 2017–2018: fifteen methods", subtitle="AUD m; MAPE in %"))
```

How to read it: only three of the other fourteen methods beat the seasonal naive (67.2): the log regression (54.5), ETS (63.0) and the regression in levels (67.0, about as good). The December trap: naive repeats the December 2016 peak (3,330.5) for every month and drift even adds 18.81 a month, so both forecast far too high (mean errors −1,275.8 and −1,510.9).

## Step 8: the 2019 forecast with 95 % bands

The winner is refitted on all 120 months and forecasts 2019 (slide 27). The 95 % band (`obs_ci_lower`, `obs_ci_upper`) should hold the actual value in 95 of 100 months; SARIMA gives its own band.

```{python}
# refit on 2009-2018 and forecast 2019 with 95 % bands
reg120 = smf.ols("np.log(value) ~ t + C(m)", data=d).fit()
new = pl.DataFrame({"t": range(121, 133), "m": range(1, 13)}).to_pandas()
band = reg120.get_prediction(new).summary_frame(alpha=0.05)
sar120 = tsa.SARIMAX(np.log(y), order=(0, 1, 1), seasonal_order=(0, 1, 1, 12)).fit(disp=0)
sar_band = sar120.get_forecast(12).conf_int(alpha=0.05)
f2019 = pl.DataFrame({"month": df["month"].tail(12).dt.offset_by("1y"),
                      "forecast": np.exp(band["mean"]), "low": np.exp(band["obs_ci_lower"]),
                      "high": np.exp(band["obs_ci_upper"]), "sarima": np.exp(sar120.forecast(12)),
                      "sarima_low": np.exp(sar_band[:, 0]), "sarima_high": np.exp(sar_band[:, 1])})
print("2019 total:", round(f2019["forecast"].sum()), " 2018:", round(totals[-1]))
f2019.with_columns(pl.col(pl.Float64).round(1))
```

January–April 2019 are in the file but were never used: the check.

```{python}
# the actual January-April 2019 against the band
full = pl.read_csv("../../data/forecasting/aus_clothing_retail.csv", try_parse_dates=True)
check = (full.join(f2019, on="month")
         .with_columns(error=pl.col("value") - pl.col("forecast"),
                       inside=pl.col("value").is_between("low", "high")))
print("MAE:", round(check["error"].abs().mean(), 1),
      " MAPE %:", round((100 * check["error"].abs() / check["value"]).mean(), 1))
ets120 = tsa.ETSModel(y, error="mul", trend="add", seasonal="mul", seasonal_periods=12).fit(disp=False)
print("ETS, December 2019:", ets120.forecast(12)[-1].round(1))
check.select("month", "value", "forecast", "low", "high", "inside").with_columns(pl.col(pl.Float64).round(1))
```

```{python}
# sales 2016-2018, the 2019 forecast with its band, the actual Jan-Apr 2019
from plotnine import geom_point, geom_ribbon
(ggplot(f2019, aes("month"))
 + geom_ribbon(aes(ymin="low", ymax="high"), fill="#0096D3", alpha=0.2)
 + geom_line(aes(y="forecast"), color="#0096D3", linetype="dashed")
 + geom_line(aes(y="value"), data=df.filter(pl.col("month").dt.year() >= 2016))
 + geom_point(aes(y="value"), data=check)
 + labs(x="", y="Turnover, AUD m"))
```

How to read it: plan with 3,430 AUD m for December 2019 (95 % band 3,178 to 3,702) and 25,595 for the year; January–April 2019 all fell inside the band (MAPE 1.0 %). exp() of a log forecast gives the median, not the mean; the deck does not correct for this.

## Step 9: are the errors autocorrelated?

A residual is the error of the fitted model on the training months (slide 28). Autocorrelation is their correlation with the month before; Durbin–Watson (DW) is 2 without autocorrelation and far below 2 when errors stick together; Ljung–Box tests the first lags together.

```{python}
# Durbin-Watson, lag-1 autocorrelation and Ljung-Box of the residuals
from statsmodels.stats.diagnostic import acorr_ljungbox
from statsmodels.stats.stattools import durbin_watson
r = reg.resid.to_numpy()                 # log regression of Step 3, 96 training months
r_sar = sar.resid[13:]                   # SARIMA of Step 2, after the two differences
print("log regression: DW", round(durbin_watson(r), 2), " lag-1 autocorrelation", round(tsa.acf(r)[1], 2))
print(acorr_ljungbox(r, lags=[12]))
print("SARIMA: lag-1 autocorrelation", round(tsa.acf(r_sar)[1], 2))
print(acorr_ljungbox(r_sar, lags=[24]))
f2019.select(width=(pl.col("high") - pl.col("low")).round(1),
             sarima_width=(pl.col("sarima_high") - pl.col("sarima_low")).round(1))[[0, -1]]
```

The residuals of the log regression over time, in % (on the log scale, exp(r) − 1), and their longest run of the same sign:

```{python}
# the residuals over time and the longest run of the same sign
from plotnine import geom_col
resid = (pl.DataFrame({"month": df["month"].head(96), "residual": 100 * (np.exp(r) - 1)})
         .with_columns(run=(pl.col("residual") > 0).rle_id()))
print(resid.group_by("run")
      .agg(months=pl.len(), first=pl.col("month").first(), last=pl.col("month").last())
      .sort("months").tail(1))
(ggplot(resid, aes("month", "residual")) + geom_col() + labs(x="", y="Residual, %"))
```

How to read it: the log regression's errors stick together (DW 0.49, lag-1 autocorrelation 0.72, 20 months in a row below zero), SARIMA's do not (−0.05, Ljung–Box p 0.265). So the regression band keeps almost the same width (308.6 in January, 524.0 in December) while SARIMA's widens from 209.2 to 589.1: trust the regression's point forecast, but plan later months with the SARIMA band.

## Appendix: open data for practice

Three open sources for your own forecasting practice (slide 39), none downloaded here; the textbook is Hyndman & Athanasopoulos (2021), *Forecasting: Principles and Practice*, 3rd ed., <https://otexts.com/fpp3> (Python edition <https://otexts.com/fpppy>).

- **ABS Retail Trade, Australia (8501.0)**: monthly turnover by state and industry, the source of our series; CC BY 4.0, <https://www.abs.gov.au/statistics/industry/retail-and-wholesale-trade/retail-trade-australia>.
- **Eurostat**: monthly retail trade (`sts_trtu_m`) and nights at tourist accommodation (`tour_occ_nim`) by EU country; free reuse with the source acknowledged.
- **M5 competition data (Walmart)**: daily unit sales of 3,049 products in 10 US stores, 2011–2016; the competition terms apply.
